name: Tambora
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Donohue, Mark 2007/2008. 'The Papuan Language of Tambora', Oceanic Linguistics 46(2): 520-537
earlier_scan.note: Extinct isolate known from an 1817 Raffles wordlist; Donohue's analysis (paywalled at MUSE/JSTOR) marks accents on forms like 'kalae'; Wikipedia shows the accented forms but no explicit stress rule

new_statements.quote: The function of the acute accent is not explained, but quite possibly represents erratic stress marking. [...] 3. PHONOLOGY. The phonology that we can infer is shown in table 2, consisting of 15 consonants and five vowels; suprasegmental features cannot be inferred, though if the frequent acute accents in Raffles’s list indicate stress, it appears to be penultimate. Depending on the interpretation of the hyphen there might be a glottal stop as well.
new_statements.citation: Donohue, Mark. 2007. The Papuan Language of Tambora. Oceanic Linguistics 46(2): 520-537. doi:10.1353/ol.2008.0014
new_statements.locator: p. 523 (sec. 2, paragraph preceding Table 1; and sec. 3 'Phonology', first sentence)
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only evidence is the acute accents Raffles (1817) printed on his ~48-word Tembora list, which Raffles never explains; Donohue reads them as (erratic) stress marks and observes that, if so, stress falls predominantly on the penultimate syllable (e.g. kutélin, koného, saróne, homóri, kokóre, simári, karáyi, moríhoh). He explicitly says suprasegmentals cannot be securely inferred from the corpus.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said (corpus is isolated words only).
new_statements.exceptions: None discussed by Donohue; the accent marking is called 'erratic' (some polysyllables unaccented, e.g. seena, yelai, maimpo, naido). A few accented forms in Raffles' list are not obviously penultimate depending on syllabification of vowel sequences/hyphens (kálae, báta-in, óna-yit, gónong vs gonóre), which Donohue does not comment on.
new_statements.domain_note: Citation forms only: single words elicited in 1810s and printed in a comparative vocabulary; no phrases or clauses exist for the language. Statement is an inference from a philological source, hedged as conditional.
new_statements.identity_note: Single variety; Raffles spells it 'Tembóra', Zollinger 'Tambora/Tembora'. Language extinct since the 1815 eruption; entire corpus is Raffles' 1817 ~48-word list (Appendix F, vol. II), so Donohue 2007 is and will remain the only linguistic analysis. Glottocode tamb1257, ISO xxt.

sources.note: Sec. 'Het vroegere rijk Tambora' states he repeats Raffles' list ('welke ik hieronder over zal nemen') and compares it with Ende/Flores lists; his respellings drop the accents (per Donohue's Table 1); nothing on accent or stress.

sources.citation: Raffles, Thomas Stamford. 1817. The History of Java, vol. II. London. Appendix F (continued): 'A Comparative Vocabulary of the Bugis, Makasar, Mandhar, Buton, Sasak, Bima, Sembawa, Tembora, and Ende languages', pp. cxcviii-cxcix (Wellcome scan b22012382_0002, PDF pp. 576-577)
sources.note: Primary and only wordlist (~48 items). Acute accents are printed on most polysyllables in the Tembora column (kálae, kutélin, báta-in, kúmba, koného, láli, saróne, sisaróne, simári, óna-yit, homóri, kokóre, saing'óre, saing kóme, karáyi, máng'ong, moríhoh, mákan...), verified on 220-dpi page renders; no explanation of the accent anywhere in the volume (0 hits for 'accent' in the scanned). No statement.
